newsitem.title: SWEDEN: TENNIS-EDBERG INJURY MARS OPENING DAY OF DAVIS CUP FINAL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-EDBERG INJURY MARS OPENING DAY OF DAVIS CUP FINAL.

text.p: Stefan Edberg's tennis swansong hit a painful note on Friday when he twisted his ankle in the first match of the Davis Cup final against France, leaving team mate Thomas Enqvist to haul Sweden level.
Edberg, who retires from competitive tennis after the tie, lost 6-3 6-4 6-3 to Cedric Pioline after being wrong-footed by a pass and falling heavily in the sixth game of the first set.
He played the rest of the match with a limp and said afterwards he did not know whether he would be fit for Sunday's reverse singles.
Enqvist, the highest ranked player in the final at number nine in the world, had little trouble holding off the challenge of Arnaud Boetsch, winning 6-4 6-3 7-6 to level the tie 1-1.
Edberg took a three-minute injury break after his fall and had his right ankle tightly strapped. But it caused him obvious discomfort and any quick or heavy movement made him wince with pain.
"I did what I could," he said gloomily afterwards. "It was a question of hanging in there and waiting for miracles -- but they did not come.
"I was in pain. I could not move at all like I should," added Edberg, who has beaten Pioline at their last four meetings, the most recent at the Italian Open in May this year.
Edberg, winner of six grand slam titles in a 14-year professional career said he would have to rest his swollen ankle on Saturday and hope it improved.
"If I'm not very nearly 100 percent fit it's not fair on myself or the others. It's better to have someone healthy," he said.
If Edberg is unable to play, one of the Swedish doubles team of Jonas Bjorkman and Nicklas Kulti will deputise against Boetsch on Sunday.
Pioline kept Edberg running, forcing balls wide and long. He won the match with a deftly placed lob that the Swede, who is 31 next month, had no chance of retrieving.
"Despite feeling sympathy for him, I could not show pity," Pioline said.
"It's a bit upsetting but you have to try to forget that and concentrate on the game."
Both French players enjoyed raucous support from a noisy contingent of some 600 supporters decked in red, white and blue hats and scarves and armed with hooters and whistles.
Their cries echoed around the converted ship-building shed used for the tie, often drowning out the more measured Swedish applause.
The noise reached a crescendo when Boetsch, struggling against the lanky Enqvist's power and confidence, forced a third set tie-break.
But Boetsch, ranked 33 in the world and possessing nothing like Enqvist's range of shots, succumbed 7-2, bowing out with an ill-judged forehand into the net.
Enqvist, heralded by the Swedish media as Edberg's natural successor, is on a high after winning two end-of-season tournaments, the Paris and Swedish Opens.
"I didn't feel that much pressure even after Stefan's match," he said. "I went out there had a lot of fun and played some good tennis."
Sweden's non-playing captain Karl Axel Hageskog said he did not have to decide whether Edberg would play until an hour before Sunday's matches.
"He has a slghtly torn ligament. We have put some pressure on it and we will see what happens," Hakeskog said.
For Edberg the wait will be hard to bear. "I do not yet know whether that was my last ever match or not," he said.
